vignette: Mohammed Al-Sayed is a 75-year-old sculptor from Baghdad, who lost his wife of fifty years just last year. Now widowed and living alone in the same modest apartment they shared for decades, Mohammed often finds himself wandering through memories filled with both warmth and sorrow. His days are now spent mostly in solitude within his cluttered studio, surrounded by unfinished sculptures and a few pieces he has recently completed. The turning point in Mohammed's life came nearly two years ago when he was involved in a near-fatal car accident on his way back from a gallery opening where one of his sculptures was exhibited. The night was dark, with rain making the streets slick, when another vehicle lost control and slammed into him head-on. He spent weeks in the hospital recovering from multiple fractures and internal injuries. Since then, Mohammed has been haunted by persistent flashbacks and recurring nightmares that vividly replay the terrifying moments of that collision. In his studio, Mohammed often pauses mid-sculpture as a wave of panic engulfs him, reminiscent of the moment he heard the screeching tires and felt the impact. His hands tremble, and he can almost feel the pressure on his chest again, making it hard for him to breathe. These episodes are so intense that sometimes he has to stop working entirely and step outside into the fresh air just to regain a sense of calm. During these bouts of anxiety, Mohammed frequently checks if all doors in his studio are locked and reinforced with additional locks. He believes this will keep him safe from intruders or other potential dangers, even though logically he understands that such precautions might be excessive. His sculptures often reflect the tumultuous emotional landscape he navigates daily; some pieces are fragmented and disjointed, mirroring his internal chaos. Mohammed's nights are particularly difficult. Nightmares of being trapped in a crushing space force him to wake up drenched in sweat, gasping for air. These nightmares have made it challenging for Mohammed to get adequate sleep, often leaving him feeling exhausted and irritable during the day. He has grown increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings and family events out of fear that another traumatic event might occur. His interactions with his adult children are strained as they worry about his declining health and mental well-being. They've encouraged him to seek professional help but Mohammed is hesitant, fearing it will further isolate him from the world he feels is becoming increasingly hostile and unpredictable. His sculpture work has become a form of coping mechanism; through shaping clay and stone, he finds temporary relief from the overwhelming emotions. Recently, small triggers like the sound of car horns or the sight of a red sports car remind Mohammed of his accident. These moments can send him into a state of hypervigilance, where he constantly scans his surroundings for potential threats. His once vibrant community involvement has dwindled to almost nothing; he avoids driving and limits his outings, opting instead to stay inside his studio or home. Despite these challenges, there are moments when Mohammed's creativity surges through him like a river flowing back into its bed after being dammed. In those instances, he manages to channel his emotional turmoil into his art, creating sculptures that speak volumes about resilience and endurance. His work has become more expressive, capturing the raw intensity of human experience in ways that are deeply moving. Though Mohammed's life is now overshadowed by the trauma of his accident, he clings to the hope that through his art, he can find a way to navigate this new reality with some measure of peace and acceptance.
